title: Documentation
in30Seconds: Documentation is the written record of a patient's care — the assessments, medications, treatments, and responses that go into the chart. It matters for three reasons: it keeps care continuous as patients move between shifts and settings, it is how the care team communicates, and it is the legal record of what happened. Good charting is accurate, timely, complete, and objective. The saying runs through nursing: if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done.
whyItMatters: Students meet documentation on their first clinical day, because nearly everything a nurse does ends in an entry. Get it right and the record becomes a bridge: the night nurse picks up where the day nurse left off, a new unit understands the patient before walking in, and a question asked months later about the care can be answered from the chart. Get it wrong — late entries, vague words, opinions in place of facts — and the record misleads the team and weakens the legal record. For a student, learning the four principles now is cheaper than unlearning bad habits later, and the habit transfers beyond nursing: clear, factual, timely records are the backbone of any profession that keeps them.
learningObjectives: Define documentation as the written or electronic record of a patient's care, following the ANA's principles for nursing documentation.
Explain three purposes of documentation: continuity of care, communication within the care team, and the legal record.
Apply the four documentation principles — accurate, timely, complete, objective — by evaluating example chart entries.
Identify the main chart types: the admission record, progress notes, the medication administration record, and the discharge record.
Describe the electronic health record in simple terms as the digital version of the patient's chart.
Distinguish acceptable charting from what to avoid: opinions, vague words, and corrections that erase.

collegeVersion.heading: What documentation is
collegeVersion.body: Documentation is the written record of a patient's care. In practice that means the assessments, the medications given, the treatments performed, the education provided, and the patient's responses — all recorded in the patient's chart. The American Nurses Association's Principles for Nursing Documentation (2010), which OpenStax's Fundamentals of Nursing presents, describes documentation as the record nurses create of their work, used by the care team, payors, and the legal system, and frames high-quality documentation as clear, accurate, and accessible — an essential element of safe, quality, evidence-based nursing practice. Two features carry the weight. First, it is a record: it exists so that care does not vanish when the shift ends. Second, it belongs to the patient's story: it is written for everyone who will care for that person next, not for the person who wrote it.

collegeVersion.heading: Why it matters
collegeVersion.body: Three purposes carry the lesson. Continuity: accurate documentation gives the next caregiver a comprehensive understanding of the patient's history, current condition, and the care already received, so the night nurse, the new unit, and the follow-up visit all start informed. Communication: the chart keeps every member of the health care team aware of the patient's current status and recent changes, even those with no direct contact with the patient. Legal record: documentation serves medical and legal purposes — OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills notes that documentation of medication administration is part of the patient's legal medical record and may be used when legal action is initiated, and the ANA warns that incomplete, inaccurate, or untimely records can impede legal fact-finding. Nursing culture captures all of this in a saying: if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done. Read as a professional rule rather than a literal statement, it means the record is the evidence of the care — what the team, the regulators, and the courts can point to.

collegeVersion.heading: The four principles
collegeVersion.body: Accurate — record what actually happened, with the right details: "Administered furosemide 40 mg orally at 0800" rather than "gave the water pill this morning." Timely — chart as care happens; OpenStax's Fundamentals of Nursing states that charting in real time is necessary for accurate, up-to-date records, so the 0800 medication appears in the 0800 chart, not the 1600 one. Complete — describe what was done and how the patient responded: "Cleaned wound with saline, applied new dressing, patient reported pain 3/10 during the change" rather than "wound care performed." Objective — record the facts, what the patient said and did, not your verdict: "Patient stated, 'I don't want the medication,' and turned away" rather than "patient is difficult and noncompliant." The ANA adds that every entry must be authenticated — the author identified, nothing added or inserted — and dated, time-stamped, and made in a standardized way.

collegeVersion.heading: The record's parts, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The chart is not one document but a set of records. The admission record is the initial record upon admission — medical history, medications, allergies, reason for admission. Progress notes (narrative notes) give a detailed account of the patient's condition, care, and response. The medication administration record (MAR) tracks each drug: dose, route, time, who administered it, and who ordered it. The discharge record summarizes the stay so the next setting — home, rehab, another facility — continues informed. Today most of these live in an electronic health record (EHR), which the U.S. Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT describes as a digital version of the patient's paper chart: a real-time, patient-centered record that brings together medical history, diagnoses, medications, allergies, and test results, and can be created and consulted by authorized providers across more than one organization. The honest framing: documentation is sometimes felt as paperwork that steals time from patients, but it is the care story that outlives the shift — the one place where what happened, and how the patient responded, is preserved. A chart written accurately, timely, completely, and objectively is care that keeps working after you leave the room.

vocabulary.definition: The written or electronic record of a patient's care — the assessments, medications, treatments, education, and responses kept in the patient's chart.
The patient's record, paper or electronic, in which the care provided is documented.
The initial record made upon admission, including medical history, medications, allergies, and the reason for admission.
Entries that give a running, detailed account of the patient's condition, the care provided, and the response to it; also called narrative notes.
The record that tracks each medication given: the drug, dose, route, time, who administered it, and who ordered it.
The summary of a hospital stay that tells the next care setting what happened and what to watch for.
A digital version of the patient's paper chart: a real-time, patient-centered record accessible to authorized providers, often across organizations.
Based on observable facts — what was seen, heard, said, or measured — rather than opinions or judgments.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Documentation is writing the care down. Every time a nurse checks on a patient, gives a medication, or teaches something, the important part goes into the chart: what was done, when, and how the patient responded. The chart is the memory of the shift. It lets the next nurse take over without losing anything, tells the rest of the care team what is happening, and stands as the official record if anyone ever asks what happened. Because the chart is the record of care, the professional rule is simple: if it wasn't written down, it counts as not done. So nurses chart what they do, chart it when they do it, and write facts, not opinions.
eli10.analogy: Think of a ship's log. The captain and crew keep the log so the next watch knows exactly what happened — course changes, weather, problems, and fixes — even though the crew that lived it has gone below deck. The log does not steer the ship; it makes sure the ship's story survives the watch. A patient chart is the ship's log of care: the day shift hands the night shift a record, not a rumor.
eli10.analogyLimits: A ship's log records one voyage with one crew, while a patient's chart is built by many people — nurses, providers, therapists — over the whole stay, and it is a legal document that can be used in court. Also, the log's writers rarely face questions about what they did not write; in health care, the gaps in the record are exactly what get questioned.

workedExample: At 0700, nurse Priya takes over care for Mr. Okafor, who had knee surgery the day before. The night nurse's notes tell her the story: vital signs stable at 0430, morphine 2 mg IV at 0200 for pain rated 6/10, patient slept afterward. At 0730 Priya checks the incision — clean, dry, dressing intact — and charts it, with her initials and the time, before giving the morning medications. When she records the acetaminophen she administers, she writes the dose, route, and time into the MAR. By the end of her shift, the afternoon nurse can read exactly what happened during Priya's eight hours: assessments done, medications given, the patient's response, and the plan for the evening. Nothing about the shift was dramatic; everything about it was written down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Charting "patient had a good day" or "wound care performed" instead of describing what happened.
commonMistakes.correction: Vague words cannot be verified later. Write the specifics: what was done, when, and how the patient responded — for example, "Ambulates to the bathroom with standby assist; incision dry and intact."

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing opinions as facts — "patient seems fine" or "patient is lazy."
commonMistakes.correction: Record observable facts and the patient's own words: "Patient stated, 'I feel fine'" and "Patient declined to walk today, stating he felt tired." The chart documents what happened, not your verdict on it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Correcting a paper error by erasing it or covering it with correction fluid.
commonMistakes.correction: Draw a single line through the error, add the date and your initials, and write the correct entry. The original entry stays visible, which is what keeps the record honest.

Chart as close to the care as possible. Late entries invite error and make the record look reconstructed rather than kept. If an entry is unavoidably late, follow your agency's policy for late entries.

commonMistakes.mistake: Signing an entry for someone else's care, or leaving an entry unsigned.
commonMistakes.correction: Every entry must be authenticated: the author identified, dated, and time-stamped. Sign only what you did — the record must show who did what.

compareContrast.distinction: Progress notes tell the story of the patient's condition and care in narrative form; the MAR is a structured record of each medication — drug, dose, route, time, and who administered and ordered it. One answers "what is happening with this patient?", the other "exactly what was given, and when?"

A paper chart is a physical folder of forms; an EHR is the digital version — a real-time, patient-centered record that authorized providers can consult across organizations. Both hold the same kinds of entries; the EHR makes them shareable instantly.

An objective entry records what was observed — the patient's words, vital signs, behavior; an opinion interprets or judges — "noncompliant," "difficult." The chart documents facts; judgments belong in clinical discussion, not the record.

keyTakeaway: Documentation is the care story that outlives the shift: the written record of what was done, when, and how the patient responded. Chart accurately, timely, completely, and objectively — because if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student asks an instructor, "What is documentation, exactly?" Which answer matches how nursing texts describe it?
options: The verbal report a nurse gives to the next shift at handoff.
The written or electronic record of a patient's care, including assessments, medications, treatments, and responses.
The list of diagnoses the provider writes on the admission form.
The insurance bill generated from the hospital stay.
questionBank.explanation: Documentation is the record of the patient's care — assessments, medications, treatments, education, and responses — kept in the chart, as described in OpenStax's Fundamentals of Nursing and the ANA's principles. A verbal handoff is communication, not a record; diagnoses and bills are contents of the record, not documentation itself.

questionBank.prompt: A nurse gives a patient 40 mg of furosemide orally at 0800 but, because the unit got busy, charts the administration at 1600. Which documentation principle did the nurse violate?
options: Objectivity
Completeness
Timeliness
Confidentiality
questionBank.explanation: Timeliness means charting as care happens — OpenStax's Fundamentals of Nursing states that charting in real time is necessary for accurate, up-to-date patient records. Recording the medication four hours late breaks that principle. The entry's content is not inaccurate or incomplete, and confidentiality concerns protecting the record, not when it is written.

questionBank.prompt: A patient refuses a prescribed medication. Which chart entry is objective and appropriate to write?
options: Patient seems grumpy and refused the medication.
Patient is a difficult person who argues with staff.
Patient is obviously noncompliant with treatment.
Patient stated, "I don't want the medication," and turned away when it was offered.
questionBank.explanation: Objective documentation records the facts: what the patient said and did. The other options are opinions and labels — "grumpy," "difficult," "noncompliant" — which interpret and judge instead of describing. OpenStax's guidance to chart care, not conflicts, puts the patient's actual words and behavior in the record.

questionBank.prompt: While charting on a paper medication record, a nurse makes a mistake. How should the entry be corrected?
options: Draw a single line through the error, add the date and initials, and record the correct entry.
Erase the error and rewrite the correct entry in the same spot.
Cover the error with correction fluid and write over it.
Tear out the page and copy the record onto a fresh one.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills states that a mistaken paper entry is noted by drawing a single line through the error, with the date and your initials — and never by erasing, covering, or obscuring the original. The visible original is what keeps the record honest and auditable; erasing, white-out, and replacing pages destroy that integrity.

questionBank.prompt: A patient is transferred to another unit, and the receiving nurse reads the chart to plan the day's care: what was done, how the patient responded, and what still needs attention. Which purpose of documentation does this best illustrate?
options: Meeting insurance billing requirements
Continuity of care and communication within the care team
Satisfying the patient's request for a copy of the record
Creating a staffing schedule for the unit
questionBank.explanation: Accurate documentation gives subsequent caregivers a comprehensive understanding of the patient's history, current condition, and care received — that is continuity of care, and the chart is how the care team communicates with members who were not present. Billing, patient copies, and staffing are not what the receiving nurse is drawing on here.
